chapters.title: Welcome to Foundations PL4
chapters.summary: Start with one chest. Turn its contents into a useful live monitor.

sections.heading: WELCOME
sections.body: Foundations PL4 helps you see what is happening inside your storage and machines. Connect a target, read its data, then choose how a monitor should present it. A simple chest counter is enough to learn the whole loop.

sections.heading: CONNECT  /  READ  /  DISPLAY
sections.body: A Node touches the target. Data Cables carry the connection. A Reader turns the target into inventory, fluid, energy or information samples. A Display presents those samples as text, item or block pictures, grids, fluid tanks or bars.

sections.heading: BEGIN HERE
sections.body: Use the Tutorial > button below in two-page mode, or open First inventory monitor in the chapter list. The walkthrough uses a chest, 17 stone and 3 dirt, with a check after every stage. Nothing in the guide moves items, places blocks or changes your layout for you.

sections.heading: BUILD AT YOUR PACE
sections.body: After the first monitor, try From list to block icon, Your first energy monitor, Grow a large display, Hologram walkthrough and Hammer walkthrough. Network, Display and Reference tabs explain the individual components in more detail.

sections.heading: THIS EDITION
sections.body: This guide covers Foundations PL4 on Minecraft 1.21.1 / NeoForge. Practical Logistics 2 is the visual reference; the unfinished PL3 project is not the feature checklist. Some original GSI interactions and integrations are still pending. See Port status and credits for the boundaries.

sections.heading: THE GUIDE ITEM
sections.body: Craft one Minecraft book with one sapphire accepted by c:gems/sapphire. Right-click the resulting Field Guide in the air. The existing foundations_pl4:plguide ID, recipe and saved bookmarks are retained.

chapters.title: First inventory monitor
chapters.summary: A chest, two test stacks and a compact reader/display pair.

sections.heading: 1  /  WHAT YOU NEED
sections.body: For the first build, keep it simple: grab a chest, a Node, a few Data Cables, an Inventory Reader, one normal Display Screen and an Operator. A Large Display works too, but one panel is easier to learn on. Put exactly 17 stone and 3 dirt in the otherwise empty chest; those numbers give you an easy sanity check later.

sections.heading: 2  /  HOOK UP THE CHEST
sections.body: Place the Node on an exposed face of the chest, then click the Node with a Data Cable so the cable centre shares the same multipart host. Run the cable a short distance away. You should see the Node still facing the chest with a visible connector leading into the cable.

sections.heading: 3  /  GIVE THE NETWORK A READER
sections.body: Mount the Inventory Reader on the data network and leave its outward face clear for the screen. Before covering it, right-click the reader and name it chest_demo. Open Data and confirm it can already see 17 stone and 3 dirt. If those numbers are wrong, fix the Node/cable side before touching the display.

sections.heading: 4  /  SNAP ON THE SCREEN
sections.body: Click the reader's outward face with the Display Screen. The screen uses its own display slot, so it does not need a separate cable branch. Normal right-click edits the screen; empty-hand Shift-right-click still reaches the reader underneath.

sections.heading: 5  /  POINT IT AT chest_demo
sections.body: Open the screen editor, use ? for Data / Settings, and select chest_demo as the Reader. Leave View on AUTO_LIST for this first test. Close the editor and you should see the same 17 stone and 3 dirt that were visible in the reader Data tab.

sections.heading: 6  /  MAKE SURE IT IS LIVE
sections.body: Drop five more stone into the chest. After the normal sampling delay, the display should move from 17 stone to 22 stone. Remove one dirt and it should fall from 3 dirt to 2 dirt. That proves you are looking at live reader data rather than a static item picture.

sections.heading: NOT WORKING YET?
sections.body: Return to the reader Data tab first. Empty data points to the Node, machine side or cable ports. Correct reader data but an empty monitor points to reader selection, display view/page or facing. Use the Operator to check disabled ports. See Reader + display and Troubleshooting before rebuilding the entire network.

chapters.title: From list to block icon
chapters.summary: Replace automatic text with a real stone model and live quantity.

sections.heading: 1  /  OPEN THE SCREEN EDITOR
sections.body: Use the working chest_demo screen from the last tutorial. Right-click the monitor, then press + on its left toolbar. The toolbar stays on the screen while the help/key hints stay on your own HUD, so you can work close to the panel without your hand hiding the instructions. Right-click is Back throughout the editor stack.

sections.heading: 2  /  PICK A BLOCK PICTURE
sections.body: Choose Block model, select chest_demo as the Reader, then Pick the stone row. Leave Static resource blank so the element stays tied to the live reader entry. If the source is an ingot or tool rather than a block item, use Item icon instead.

sections.heading: 3  /  PLACE IT ON THE CANVAS
sections.body: Leave Quantity enabled and add the element. The screen switches to CUSTOM and opens the page that received the new element. You should now see a stone block with its live count instead of the old text-only inventory list. If the server rejects the edit, your existing layout stays untouched.

sections.heading: 4  /  MOVE AND RESIZE IT
sections.body: Click the block picture to select it. Drag the element itself to move it, or grab any bright corner bracket to resize while the opposite corner remains anchored. G toggles snapping and E opens Properties. Change the chest contents once more and make sure the quantity follows.

sections.heading: 5  /  TRY A SMALL GRID
sections.body: Add an Inventory grid with chest_demo as the Reader. New grids start at 3 columns, which is a useful size for most panels. Columns changes the real grid and the Properties screen previews the result; Offset skips earlier rows. Put it on another page if you want to compare layouts without overlap.

sections.heading: VIEW IS NOT READER MODE
sections.body: Reader data modes decide what is measured. Display View decides AUTO_LIST versus CUSTOM. Element Type decides the actual renderer. Switching to AUTO_LIST keeps the custom elements saved; switch back to CUSTOM to see them again. Saving an element to another page now reveals that page automatically.

chapters.title: Your first energy monitor
chapters.summary: Use the correct reader, machine face and unit before drawing a bar.

sections.heading: 1  /  START WITH KNOWN POWER
sections.body: Pick a charged machine or battery whose own GUI shows stored energy and capacity. Put a Node on a side that actually exposes energy; multiblocks often require a controller or power port rather than any random casing. Note the machine's numbers before you connect PL4.

sections.heading: 2  /  ADD AN ENERGY READER
sections.body: Connect an Energy Reader to the same data network and name it power_demo. AUTO is a good first choice, or choose FE, EU or J when you specifically want that provider. Compare the Reader's Data tab with the machine GUI before building a fancy screen.

sections.heading: 3  /  KEEP THE UNIT HONEST
sections.body: FE, Mekanism Joules and GTCEu EU are reported in their own units. PL4 does not silently convert them into one made-up number. A blocked side or unsupported machine should give you a diagnostic instead of pretending the battery is empty.

sections.heading: 4  /  TURN IT INTO A BAR
sections.body: On a display, choose power_demo and add a Progress / energy bar using a row that has both a current value and a capacity. Keep Quantity on if you want the number over the bar. The fill should match the percentage shown by the machine itself.

sections.heading: 5  /  WATCH IT MOVE
sections.body: Charge or drain the machine and wait for the next sample. Both the number and the bar should follow. Remember that stored/capacity is not the same thing as generation or transfer rate; use separate data when a machine exposes those values.

chapters.title: Grow a large display
chapters.summary: Extend an edge without turning the new panel sideways or losing its layout.

sections.heading: 1  /  BUILD ONE WORKING TILE
sections.body: Start with a single Large Display that already shows one custom element. It is much easier to prove expansion works when you know the original tile, reader selection and layout are healthy first.

sections.heading: 2  /  EXTEND FROM AN EDGE
sections.body: Hold another Large Display and click a thin side edge of the existing panel, or click near that edge on the front. The new tile should extend in the same plane and facing. Clicking the middle does not guess a direction; sneak-place if you deliberately want an independent panel.

sections.heading: 3  /  FILL THE RECTANGLE
sections.body: Joined displays form filled rectangles. A 2 by 2 screen needs all four positions; one extra tile beside a taller display is only an L-shape until the missing cell is filled. The supported maximum is 16 by 16 tiles. PL4 never spends extra panels automatically to complete a row.

sections.heading: 4  /  CHECK THE LAYOUT SURVIVED
sections.body: Extend left or upward so the logical top-left controller has to change, then check your original element. The shared layout should remain where you put it. Splitting a joined board leaves the pieces with the last shared settings rather than resurrecting old hidden per-tile layouts.

sections.heading: 5  /  RELOAD IT ONCE
sections.body: Save and reopen a copied world. Facing, reader selection, pages and custom positions should survive. Joining screens is visual only; it must not bridge otherwise separate machine or transfer networks.

chapters.title: Hologram walkthrough
chapters.summary: Place a projector, choose its view, then bind a real data element.

sections.heading: 1  /  START WITH WORKING DATA
sections.body: Mount a normal or Advanced Holographic Display on a supported visual connection and bind it to a reader you already know works. That way, if the projection looks wrong, you are debugging the projector rather than wondering whether the network is empty.

sections.heading: 2  /  AIM THE PROJECTOR
sections.body: For floor or ceiling mounts, Settings > View rotates the readable projection north, east, south or west. Wall projectors derive their direction from the mounting face. The flat-screen Front inward/outward option is not the hologram direction control.

sections.heading: 3  /  GIVE IT SOMETHING OBVIOUS
sections.body: Add a short Text / value or Item icon first. A simple, obvious element makes orientation and spacing easier to judge than a busy page. R17 measures projection clearance from the emitter hardware itself: normal holograms leave about 0.90 blocks from the emitter bar; Advanced leaves about 1.20 from its top emitter on floor/ceiling mounts or selected wall panel. The canvas sits directly above a floor emitter, below a ceiling emitter, or outward from a wall emitter. View rotates the text without moving that origin.

sections.heading: 4  /  WALK AROUND THE PLANE
sections.body: Look from the front, rear and a shallow side angle. Text should stay readable rather than mirror, floor/ceiling text should stay upright, and the projector/cables should no longer cut through the data plane. The projection is still a flat two-sided surface, not a volumetric object.

sections.heading: SCOPE
sections.body: Holograms stay independent rather than joining into Large Display rectangles. R17 fixes the projection origin and retains readable two-sided orientation, but it does not claim the complete historical advanced/volumetric GSI system. If something still looks wrong, report normal vs Advanced, mounting face and View direction.

chapters.title: Hammer walkthrough
chapters.summary: Use the three-block machine and its actual two-slot inventory.

sections.heading: 1  /  GIVE IT ROOM TO SWING
sections.body: Place the Forging Hammer with two clear air blocks above the base. Those upper cells belong to the hammer structure. If an older hammer is obstructed, it pauses instead of deleting the blocks above it.

sections.heading: 2  /  OPEN THE HAMMER
sections.body: Right-click the base or either upper piece. The GUI has a real input slot, output slot and your inventory; you do not need to hand-feed or hand-extract items the way the early port did.

sections.heading: 3  /  TRY THE DEFAULT RECIPE
sections.body: Put one item accepted by c:stones into the input. With the default datapack this produces four stone plates. Recipe counts, processing time and cooldown are data-driven, so a modpack or KubeJS script may intentionally change the result.

sections.heading: 4  /  LET THE CYCLE FINISH
sections.body: Watch the progress arrow and hammer head, then collect the output after the cycle. A full or incompatible output must stop processing without eating another input. Cooldown finishes before the next strike begins.

sections.heading: 5  /  THEN AUTOMATE IT
sections.body: Once the manual cycle works, try a hopper or your preferred supported pipe: automation inserts into input and extracts from output. Prove the simple route first before burying the hammer inside a larger logistics chain.

chapters.title: Using the Field Guide
chapters.summary: Search, tabs, bookmarks and readable pages.

sections.heading: NAVIGATION
sections.body: The four side tabs group chapters into Welcome and tutorials, Networks, Displays and Reference. A section click clears search/bookmark filters and selects a chapter in that section, so the right page cannot silently remain on an unrelated chapter. Select a chapter on the left; each pane scrolls separately. Welcome returns to the landing page; its Tutorial > button starts the inventory walkthrough. Home also returns to Welcome when search is not focused.

sections.heading: SEARCH AND BOOKMARKS
sections.body: Search matches chapter titles, summaries and body text across all chapters. Clear the search to return to the selected section. The star bookmarks the selected chapter; Bookmarks highlights when only saved chapters are shown. The last chapter and bookmarks are stored on this client only. Hover a chapter to read its summary below the list, without a tooltip covering either page.

sections.heading: SMALL WINDOWS
sections.body: At narrow GUI widths, Contents switches between the chapter list and reading page instead of shrinking the text. Drag a scrollbar thumb, click its track or use the mouse wheel. Escape closes the guide, including while Search has focus.

chapters.title: Reader + display
chapters.summary: A compact same-face assembly without a cable detour.

sections.heading: MOUNT THE PANEL
sections.body: Click the outward face of a reader with a normal, mini or large display. It uses a separate display slot, leaving the reader in place. The screen should be viewed from that outward side.

sections.heading: ACCESS THE READER
sections.body: Right-click opens the on-screen editor; ? opens Data / Settings. Shift-right-click with an empty hand opens the reader underneath. Sneak-use the Operator on the front panel to remove that component without deliberately breaking the entire host.

sections.heading: INPUT IS NOT OUTPUT
sections.body: A reader takes machine-network input behind it. Its front carries visual output. A cable on the front may feed remote displays, but is not a bridge for machine access or item/fluid/energy transfers.

sections.heading: NO EXTRA BRANCH REQUIRED
sections.body: A same-face reader/panel pair does not require a cable loop around its front. A bare reader can use an exposed compatible cable in the adjacent block behind it. A disabled or obstructed local cable port cannot be bypassed by that external connection.

chapters.title: Nodes and targets
chapters.summary: Attach the network to a real machine interface.

sections.heading: MACHINE CONNECTION
sections.body: A Node identifies the block on its mounted side as a data target. Attach it to the chest, tank, battery or machine face you intend to inspect, then connect the Node to Data Cable.

sections.heading: SIDED ACCESS
sections.body: The connected face matters. A modded machine may expose inventory, fluid or energy only on particular sides or ports. PL4 does not secretly scan every side or bypass a disabled side configuration.

sections.heading: MULTIBLOCKS
sections.body: Use a supported port or controller rather than an arbitrary casing. Two different casing blocks can expose the same underlying store; one Node at the authoritative port avoids double counting.

sections.heading: UNLOADED TARGETS
sections.body: PL4 observes loaded targets and does not force-load chunks. Restore the loaded connection before expecting live rows.

chapters.title: Cables and ports
chapters.summary: Directional multipart wiring and operator controls.

sections.heading: TWO CABLE FAMILIES
sections.body: Data Cable carries the machine data network. Redstone Cable carries its redstone network. The families do not connect interchangeably.

sections.heading: LOCAL AND EXTERNAL PORTS
sections.body: A compatible cable centre can share a host with face components. Exposed compatible external component ports may also connect to an adjacent cable. Merely touching sideways is not a port. Reader network input and visual output are separate.

sections.heading: OPERATOR
sections.body: Right-click a cable arm with the Operator to disable or re-enable that port. When permitted, the corresponding neighbor cable port is toggled too. Sneak-right-click removes one selected component; its settings and pending transfer state stay with its dropped item.

sections.heading: BLOCKING AND OWNERSHIP
sections.body: An occupied face, disabled port, different cable family, overlapping part or protected position can reject placement or connection. Do not defeat this by routing a cable through the same blocked face.

sections.heading: DATA FIRST
sections.body: Open Data on the Inventory Reader before configuring a display. It lists supported item-handler inventories reached through Nodes. Click a data row to copy its key for a display element.

body.heading: NO ROWS
body.body: Check the reader Data tab, output direction, cable family and disabled ports. Check the display selected reader name. A larger screen with no supported source is still an empty screen.

sections.title: Forging Hammer
sections.summary: Three-block machine with a native inventory.

sections.heading: PLACE THE MACHINE
sections.body: Leave two clear air blocks above the base. The hammer occupies a three-block-tall structure. Placement must not replace a roof or other obstruction. An obstructed older hammer pauses and preserves inventory.

sections.heading: USE THE INVENTORY
sections.body: Right-click the base or either upper part. Put an ingredient in the left slot; collect the result at the right. Shift-click moves compatible stacks. The arrow shows processing progress; cooldown returns the hammer before another stroke.

sections.heading: AUTOMATION AND REMOVAL
sections.body: Automation inserts input and extracts output. The result slot rejects insertion. Removing an upper part dismantles the base; take normal precautions with machine inventory. The upper structure parts have no separate item drops.

sections.heading: RECIPE TIMES
sections.body: Bundled recipes use 100 processing ticks and 200 cooldown ticks. A datapack or KubeJS custom recipe can change those durations. The currently active recipe data is authoritative.

sections.title: Materials and recipes
sections.summary: Sapphires, plates and the guide recipe.

sections.heading: SAPPHIRE
sections.body: The port registers sapphire ore, sapphire and sapphire dust. Overworld generation is configured in its datapack world-generation resources; it is not a promise to match every historical vein rule.

sections.heading: BUNDLED FORGING
sections.body:
1 tagged stone -> 4 Stone Plates.
1 tagged diamond -> 4 Etched Plates.
1 tagged redstone dust -> 4 Signalling Plates.
1 tagged ender pearl -> 4 Wireless Plates.
1 tagged sapphire -> 1 Sapphire Dust.
1 tagged sapphire ore -> 2 Sapphire Dust.

sections.heading: FIELD GUIDE
sections.body: Combine a book and a tagged sapphire gem in a crafting grid. The result is the Foundations PL4 Field Guide. Pack recipes can override these defaults; consult the active recipe data.

sections.title: Wireless links and Arrays
sections.summary: Bind explicit targets without an external core.

sections.heading: EMITTER TO RECEIVER
sections.body: Sneak-right-click one of your data emitters with a Transceiver to bind it, then right-click a matching receiver. Redstone emitters/receivers use their matching family. Ownership and configured wireless permissions still apply.

sections.heading: ARRAY
sections.body: Sneak-right-click a block target to bind its position/side, then use the bound tool on an Array. The port supports up to eight saved links. It does not reproduce the original eight physical transceiver inventory slots.

sections.heading: ENTITY LINK
sections.body: Use the Entity Transceiver on a living entity to bind its identity, then add a supported link to an Entity Node or Array. An unlinked Entity Node can supply a nearby-entity count.

sections.heading: LOADED WORLDS
sections.body: Cross-dimension wireless is configurable. Linked targets still need to be loaded; PL4 does not force-load them. Clear links through component Settings when replacing a target.

sections.heading: WIRELESS STORAGE
sections.body: Wireless Storage currently opens a bound-target read-only view. It is not a complete remote inventory management system.

sections.title: Transfer Nodes
sections.summary: Move items, fluids and FE through the data network without turning ordinary Nodes into pumps.

sections.heading: THE SIMPLE PAIR
sections.body: For the most explicit setup, put a Transfer Node on the source and set it to REMOVE / EXPORT. Put another Transfer Node on the destination and set it to ADD / IMPORT. Connect both to the same data network. The REMOVE side extracts; the ADD side accepts. Explicit ADD destinations are preferred over ordinary Nodes when priorities tie.

sections.heading: NORMAL NODES ARE ENDPOINTS
sections.body: R16 restores the useful PL2-style network pool. A normal Node attached to a chest, tank or FE machine can be a passive endpoint. An ADD Transfer Node can import from normal Nodes on its data network. A REMOVE Transfer Node can export into normal Nodes. Normal Node to normal Node never moves resources by itself; a Transfer Node must drive the operation.

sections.heading: MODES
sections.body: PASSIVE moves nothing. ADD / IMPORT fills the block attached to that Transfer Node from eligible network sources. REMOVE / EXPORT drains the attached block into eligible network destinations. ADD / REMOVE remains explicit-peer only in this alpha because the old PL2 directional channel/filter editor is not fully restored; this avoids blind passive-network ping-pong.

sections.heading: FILTERS, PRIORITY AND RATES
sections.body: Items and fluids use the Transfer Node filter on the direction that node controls. Higher-priority explicit Transfer Nodes are considered first; equal-priority endpoints rotate deterministically. Default per-cycle caps remain 64 items, 1000 mB and 10000 FE. A full destination is simulated before extraction, so it should not consume the source.

sections.heading: SAFETY AND ESCROW
sections.body: If a real provider accepts less than simulation promised, the driving Transfer Node keeps the remainder in persistent escrow and retries later. Resources inserted during a transfer cycle are not immediately re-extracted in that same cycle. Operator removal preserves pending escrow. Items, compatible fluid handlers and FE are transportable; native EU and Mekanism Joule support remains read-only telemetry in this alpha.

sections.title: Redstone and clocks
sections.summary: Signal networks and simple numeric conditions.

sections.heading: SIGNAL NETWORK
sections.body: Redstone Nodes/emitters sample supported redstone inputs. Redstone Cable and receivers propagate sampled signals on their separate network.

sections.heading: SIGNALLER
sections.body: The Redstone Signaller evaluates a selected numeric reader row using its comparison and threshold. A true condition produces a signal. This is a single condition, not the full original multi-statement logic editor.

sections.heading: CLOCK
sections.body: A clock uses the Interval setting in ticks. The port samples/pulses with the network update cadence; very short requested timing is bounded. World-time rows are not wall-clock time.

sections.title: Troubleshooting
sections.summary: Start with data, then connections, then presentation.

sections.heading: READER IS EMPTY
sections.body: Check the Node target and exposed side. Inspect cable family, occupied faces, blocked ports and loaded chunks. Confirm the correct reader type. Test a simple chest or known FE battery before a complex multiblock.

sections.heading: DISPLAY IS EMPTY
sections.body: Read the reader Data tab first. Check Reader name or use automatic selection. Confirm the compact pair or correctly sided visual route. In CUSTOM mode check the selected page and element bindings; an empty custom layout intentionally stays blank. In AUTO_LIST mode only the automatic table is shown. Large-screen adjacency does not supply data by itself.

sections.heading: SCREEN FACES THE WRONG WAY
sections.body: For flat panels change Front in Settings. For floor/ceiling holograms use View. Do not rotate the entire cable network to compensate for a viewing-side setting.

sections.heading: SCREEN WILL NOT EXPAND
sections.body: Use a Large Display on the side/rim of another Large Display without sneaking. Match owner, plane and front. Complete the rectangle; remove holes. Stay within 16x16. A protected or occupied destination is intentionally rejected.

sections.heading: HAMMER DOES NOTHING
sections.body: Check two-block headroom, a valid active forging recipe, room in the output slot and cooldown. Recipe overrides can change ingredients, counts and processing time.

sections.heading: REPORTING A BUG
sections.body: Record PL4 revision, Minecraft/NeoForge versions, relevant other-mod versions and exact machine/side. Include a screenshot of the wiring, reader Data/Settings and the relevant log exception.

sections.heading: WRONG DISPLAY TYPE
sections.body: Reader Data mode chooses which rows are sampled. Display element Type chooses the graphical renderer. Use + > Type > Pick data > Add element, not just a reader mode change. Block model requires a block item; Item needs an item picture; Fluid needs a fluid sample; Bar requires positive capacity. STORAGE is numeric and cannot become an inventory picture. An unavailable selection is not silently replaced with an inventory list.

sections.heading: EDIT REJECTED
sections.body: A different player, screen expansion or settings change may advance the layout revision while properties are open. Close/reopen properties to review the newer layout before retrying. Disabled editing can also mean ownership, protection, distance, an unloaded or replaced tile, or a busy edit limit. No source/network access is granted by entering an arbitrary reader name.

sections.title: KubeJS and datapacks
sections.summary: Data recipes are supported; custom PL4 events are not.

sections.heading: SUPPORTED LAYER
sections.body: Registered items, tags, crafting JSON and the foundations_pl4:forging_hammer recipe codec can be configured through datapacks. KubeJS ServerEvents.recipes with event.custom can submit that same recipe JSON.

sections.heading: HAMMER FIELDS
sections.body: Use type, ingredient, input_count, result, processing_ticks and cooldown_ticks. In 1.21.1 the result uses id and count. The included examples/kubejs/server_scripts/pl4_recipes.js.example shows a deliberate recipe replacement.

sections.heading: OPT IN
sections.body: The updater does not install or enable KubeJS scripts. Copy and rename the example only when deliberately changing that instance/server recipe. Reload and test using your installed KubeJS version.

sections.heading: NOT A PL4 SCRIPTING API
sections.body: There is no PL4Events event group, scripted display controller, custom energy-provider registration API or dedicated recipe-builder DSL. Do not treat generic custom-recipe support as those missing integrations.

sections.heading: NETWORK
sections.body: updateTicks sets the sample/transfer interval; default 20 ticks. maximumHosts defaults to 4096 and stops an oversized network safely. maximumRows defaults to 128 synchronized reader rows. The automatic world display shows up to 24 rows when the physical panel height permits; inspect Data for the full received list.

sections.heading: TRANSFERS
sections.body: Default per-cycle limits are 64 items, 1000 millibuckets and 10000 FE. The enabled option can disable transfers. These are caps, not measured throughput guarantees.

sections.heading: OPTIONAL READERS
sections.body: energyReader.mekanismJoules and energyReader.gregtechEU enable optional native read-only providers. maximumContainersPerHandler bounds a handler traversal; excessive providers are rejected rather than partially counted.

sections.heading: GUIDE CONTENT
sections.body: Client resource packs may replace assets/foundations_pl4/guide/en_us.json. Content is bounded and validated when the guide opens. A malformed replacement displays a recovery page and logs the error instead of crashing the screen.

sections.heading: DISPLAY BUDGETS
sections.body: Typed layouts are limited to 32 elements, eight pages, eight explicit visible reader bindings, and 128 rendered item/fluid pictures per canvas. Preview metadata excludes nested inventories and uses a 4096-byte per-picture and 32768-byte component budget per sampled reader, plus small base-ID fallback records. The limits are safety caps, not performance benchmark results. Different energy units remain separate; PL4 does not convert or transfer EU/J.

sections.title: Port status and credits
sections.summary: PL2-style display restoration, current limits and credits.

sections.heading: ALPHA IMPLEMENTATION
sections.body: Foundations PL4 is an in-development port for Minecraft 1.21.1 / NeoForge. It bundles its own required core functionality. A separate Sonar Core or MCMultiPart runtime is not required.

sections.heading: CURRENT BOUNDARY
sections.body: This is not a completed stable 1:1 release. The port supplies typed item/block/fluid/bar renderers, a bounded world-space selection/move/resize/properties editor and eight pages. The full original GSI actions, nested containers, extraction controls, links, arbitrary large-screen shapes and historical integrations remain unfinished. Block pictures use the default block state, not a live remote block-entity renderer. Custom mod renderers still require pack-level visual acceptance.

sections.heading: VALIDATION BOUNDARY
sections.body: R11 retains the earlier connections, hammer, energy telemetry, typed display editor, expansion, hologram and onboarding work. Source checks do not prove a Minecraft build or in-game rendering. Test a copied world before committing important display layouts.

sections.heading: CREDITS
sections.body: Original Practical Logistics and relevant original assets: SonarSonic / Ollie Lansdell. Foundations PL4 port changes and Field Guide presentation are identified in the included NOTICE. Original MIT license notices remain in the source and built mod.

sections.heading: R11 LARGE CANVAS
sections.body: Joined Large Displays now use the whole connected monitor rectangle as their logical workspace instead of stretching one fixed 248-by-120 canvas. Existing typed layouts migrate proportionally when the rectangle changes so relative position and size are preserved. The world editor anchors its toolbar inside the visible screen edge and uses the expanded coordinate space. Native graphical acceptance is still required.
